learningObjectives.title: Food spoilage and contamination: enzymes, moulds, yeasts and bacterial growth
Bacterial contamination, cross-contamination and food poisoning
Principles of food safety: buying and storing food
Principles of food safety: preparation, cooking and serving temperatures

questions.q: Which four conditions do most bacteria need in order to multiply?
options: Light, oxygen, salt and acid
Warmth, moisture, food and time
Cold, dryness, sugar and time
Warmth, salt, light and vinegar
questions.explain: Bacteria need warmth, moisture, food (nutrients) and time to reproduce, which is why high-risk foods must be kept out of these conditions.

questions.q: At which temperature do most food-poisoning bacteria multiply most rapidly?
questions.explain: Around 37°C (human body temperature) provides the ideal warmth for most food-poisoning bacteria to grow quickly.

questions.q: Under ideal conditions, how do bacteria increase in number?
options: They divide in two roughly every 10-20 minutes
They lay eggs that hatch after several hours
They grow larger until they burst open
They multiply only once every 24 hours
questions.explain: Bacteria reproduce by binary fission, splitting into two about every 10-20 minutes, so numbers rise rapidly in warm conditions.

questions.q: A student cuts apples for a fruit salad and notices the pieces turn brown. Which action best prevents this enzymic browning?
options: Leaving the apples uncovered in a warm room
Coating the apple pieces in lemon juice
Sprinkling the apples with sugar and salt
Storing the apples in a sealed bag at room temperature
questions.explain: The acid in lemon juice slows the enzyme that causes cut fruit to brown when exposed to air.

questions.q: What is the role of enzymes in the spoilage of fruit and vegetables?
options: They cause produce to ripen and eventually over-ripen and decay
They kill all bacteria present on the surface
They add flavour and preserve the food
They stop the food from changing colour
questions.explain: Naturally occurring enzymes ripen fruit and vegetables and, if uncontrolled, continue working so the produce over-ripens and spoils.

questions.q: Cooked chicken has been left on the kitchen worktop at room temperature for four hours. What is the safest action?
options: Throw the chicken away as it has been in the danger zone too long
Reheat it briefly and then serve it
Put it in the fridge to use the next day
Serve it cold straight away
questions.explain: High-risk food left in the danger zone (5-63°C) for several hours may contain harmful bacteria or toxins and should be discarded.

questions.q: Which statement about mould is correct?
options: Mould is a microorganism that spoils food, though some moulds are used to make blue cheese
Mould is a bacterium that only grows in the freezer
Mould always makes food safer to eat
Mould cannot grow on bread or cheese
questions.explain: Mould is a fungus that usually spoils food, but selected moulds are deliberately used in products such as blue cheese.

questions.q: Which bacterium is the most common cause of food poisoning in the UK and is often found in raw poultry?
options: Listeria
Bacillus cereus
Campylobacter
Staphylococcus aureus
questions.explain: Campylobacter, commonly found in raw and undercooked poultry, is the leading cause of bacterial food poisoning in the UK.

questions.q: Salmonella food poisoning is most commonly associated with which foods?
options: Raw eggs and poultry
Fresh bread and pasta
Tinned vegetables
Boiled sweets
questions.explain: Salmonella is typically linked to raw or undercooked eggs and poultry, so these foods must be cooked thoroughly.

questions.q: Why is Listeria considered particularly dangerous?
options: It can continue to grow at refrigeration temperatures and is a risk to pregnant women
It is killed instantly simply by chilling food
It only grows at temperatures above 100°C
It cannot cause any illness in humans
questions.explain: Unlike many bacteria, Listeria can still multiply at fridge temperatures and poses a serious risk to pregnant women and their babies.

questions.q: Which bacterium is particularly associated with cooked rice that has been left warm and then reheated?
options: Salmonella
Bacillus cereus
Campylobacter
E. coli
questions.explain: Bacillus cereus can survive in cooked rice and produce toxins if the rice is left warm, which is why rice should be cooled and chilled quickly.

questions.q: What is meant by cross-contamination?
options: The transfer of harmful bacteria from one food, surface or utensil to another
The natural ripening of fruit caused by enzymes
The freezing of food to stop bacterial growth
The browning of cut apples exposed to air
questions.explain: Cross-contamination is the spread of bacteria between foods, hands, surfaces or equipment, often from raw to ready-to-eat foods.

questions.q: Staphylococcus aureus is commonly transferred to food from which source?
options: The skin, nose and cuts of food handlers
Frozen peas and vegetables
Cold tap water
Plain baking flour
questions.explain: Staphylococcus aureus lives on human skin, in the nose and in cuts, so good personal hygiene by food handlers helps prevent it spreading.

questions.q: What is the recommended temperature range for a domestic refrigerator?
options: -18°C or below
questions.explain: A fridge should run between 0°C and 5°C to slow the growth of bacteria on chilled foods.

questions.q: Why does storing food in a freezer at -18°C keep it safe for longer?
options: The low temperature makes bacteria dormant so they stop multiplying
The cold permanently kills all bacteria in the food
Freezing adds natural preservatives to the food
Freezing increases the moisture that bacteria need
questions.explain: Freezing does not kill bacteria but makes them dormant, so they stop multiplying until the food is defrosted.

questions.q: When packing away shopping, where should raw chicken be stored in the fridge?
options: On the top shelf, above the cooked foods
In the fridge door with the drinks
On the bottom shelf, below ready-to-eat foods
In the same container as the salad
questions.explain: Raw meat is stored on the bottom shelf so any drips cannot fall onto and contaminate ready-to-eat foods.

questions.q: What is the difference between a 'use by' and a 'best before' date?
options: 'Use by' relates to food safety, while 'best before' relates to quality
'Use by' relates to quality, while 'best before' relates to safety
Both dates mean exactly the same thing
'Best before' means the food becomes unsafe immediately after that date
questions.explain: A 'use by' date is about safety and must be observed, whereas 'best before' is about quality and food may still be safe afterwards.

questions.q: Which temperature range is known as the 'danger zone', in which bacteria multiply most easily?
options: 5°C to 63°C
0°C to 5°C
-18°C to 0°C
questions.explain: Between 5°C and 63°C bacteria multiply rapidly, so high-risk foods should be kept either below or above this range.

questions.q: When using a temperature probe to check that food is cooked, why is it inserted into the thickest part or centre of the food?
options: This is the slowest part to heat, so it confirms the whole item is cooked
This is always the hottest part of the food
It is the only place where bacteria can survive
It makes the food cook more quickly
questions.explain: The centre or thickest part heats last, so if it reaches a safe temperature the rest of the food will be cooked too.

questions.q: A temperature probe shows the centre of a chicken breast has reached 68°C. What should the cook do?
options: Serve it immediately as it is safe
Continue cooking until the centre reaches at least 75°C
Put it straight into the fridge
Add more raw chicken to the same pan
questions.explain: The core of the food should reach at least 75°C to ensure harmful bacteria are destroyed, so cooking must continue.
